lessons.title: Rent Escalation, Lock-In Periods and Tenant Quality

children.text: Two owners in the same Kharadi office building in Pune let identical units in the same month. One picks a young startup offering ₹1,10,000 a month. The other accepts ₹1,00,000 from the India office of a listed multinational. On day one, the first owner looks ₹1.2 lakh a year smarter. Fourteen months later, the startup has missed two rents, vacated, and left the unit empty for eight months. The multinational is still paying, with a 15% escalation on the way. The rent in the agreement is only the first number. How fast it grows, how long it is locked in, and who is paying it decide what you actually earn. By the end of this lesson you will be able to compare escalation structures, measure how secure a rent stream is, and put a rupee value on tenant quality.

body.text: A lease is not a rent number. It is a stream of future payments. Escalation decides how big that stream grows, the lock-in decides how long it is guaranteed, and tenant quality decides whether it arrives at all.

children.text: Escalation: How Fast the Rent Grows

markDefs.definition: A rent increase applied every year, such as 5% a year.
A larger rent increase applied at longer intervals, such as 15% every three years.

children.text: Indian leases use two main escalation structures. Residential agreements and many warehouse leases use an
annual escalation
, typically around 5%. Office and high-street retail leases often use a
step escalation
, typically 15% every three years. They sound similar. They are not.

body.title: Which pays more?
body.question: An office starts at ₹1,00,000 a month on a nine-year lease. Which escalation gives the owner more total rent over the nine years?
options: Both give exactly the same total
body.explanation: 5% a year wins by about ₹7.3 lakh. A 15% step every three years is equivalent to only about 4.77% a year compounded, and the owner also waits three years for each increase instead of getting a little more every year. The chart and table below show the difference.

body.title: Convert a step escalation
body.prompt: A Hyderabad warehouse lease offers a 10% rent increase every two years. What is the equivalent annual escalation? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 1.10^(1/2) − 1 = 1.0488 − 1 = 4.88% a year. Slightly below a straight 5% a year, and the owner waits two years for each increase.

markDefs.definition: A property whose contracted rent is above what a new tenant would pay in today's market, so rent is likely to fall when the lease ends.
Resetting rent to the current market level at renewal, which can move rent up or down.

children.text: Escalation has two limits. First, inflation: if consumer prices rise about 5% a year and rent rises 5% a year, the owner's real income is flat. Second, the market: escalations are contractual, but market rents are not. If a lease escalates faster than rents in the area, the unit becomes
over-rented
, and at renewal the tenant will push for a
mark-to-market
reset or simply move next door.

body.text: When you buy a pre-leased property, always compare the current contracted rent with what similar units nearby are renting for today. A generous escalation clause signed five years ago can make today's yield look excellent while hiding a rent cut waiting at the next renewal.

children.text: Lock-In and Notice: How Long the Rent Is Guaranteed

markDefs.definition: The advance warning, typically one to six months, that either side must give before ending a lease once any lock-in has passed.
An initial period, common in office leases, during which the tenant does interiors and pays no rent.

children.text: The lock-in is the only part of a lease where rent is truly guaranteed: if the tenant leaves early, it owes the rent for the rest of the lock-in. After that, the tenant can usually leave by giving the agreed
notice period
. A nine-year lease with a three-year lock-in is, in practice, three years of certain rent and six years of likely rent. Office leases often also start with a
rent-free fit-out period
, which delays your first rupee of income.

body.title: The life of a typical nine-year office lease

events.title: Signing and rent-free fit-out
events.description: The tenant pays the security deposit and builds out interiors. The owner earns no rent yet but still pays property tax.

events.title: Rent starts
events.description: Rent begins at the agreed base, with the lock-in clock already running from the lease start.

events.title: Lock-in ends and first 15% escalation
events.description: Rent steps up, but the tenant can now leave with notice. This is the first real renewal risk.

events.title: Second 15% escalation
events.description: Rent is now 32.25% above the starting rent. Check whether it is still in line with the market.

events.title: Lease expiry
events.description: The tenant renews at a negotiated, often market-based, rent or leaves. Vacancy and brokerage risk return in full.

markDefs.definition: Weighted average lease expiry: the average remaining lease term across tenants, weighted by the rent each one pays.

children.text: When a property has several tenants, owners and REITs measure income security with
WALE
. Every listed REIT on NSE and BSE reports it. A longer WALE means rent is contracted further into the future. Big tenants count for more, because losing them hurts more.

body.caption: Calculate a weighted lock-in the same way, using remaining lock-in years instead of remaining lease years.

body.title: Calculate WALE
body.prompt: An owner in Jaipur has three shops in one building. Shop A pays ₹60,000 a month with 6 years left on its lease. Shop B pays ₹30,000 with 2 years left. Shop C pays ₹10,000 with 1 year left. What is the WALE in years? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: WALE = (60,000 × 6 + 30,000 × 2 + 10,000 × 1) ÷ (60,000 + 30,000 + 10,000) = (3,60,000 + 60,000 + 10,000) ÷ 1,00,000 = 4.3 years. A simple average of the three lease terms would be 3 years, understating how secure the income is because the biggest tenant has the longest lease.

body.title: Decode the acronym
body.textWithBlank: In REIT reports, WALE stands for weighted average lease ___.
body.explanation: Weighted average lease expiry measures how many years of rent are still contracted, weighted by each tenant's share of rent.

children.text: Tenant Quality: Whether the Rent Arrives at All

A strong escalation and a long lock-in are worth little if the tenant cannot pay. Tenant quality is about verifiable, financial facts: stable income, a track record of paying, and reasons to stay. It is never about a tenant's religion, food habits, marital status or where they come from, none of which predict whether rent will be paid.

columns.label: Residential tenant
points: Verified employment and salary slips, or an employer-signed company lease
A reference from a previous landlord confirming on-time rent
Rent comfortably within about a third of take-home pay
PAN, Aadhaar and police verification completed
Plans to stay: school admissions nearby, a long commute saved

columns.label: Commercial tenant
points: Several years of filed financial statements showing profits and cash
A credit rating from CRISIL, ICRA or CARE, or a parent company guarantee
Active GST registration and a business with a long operating history
Heavy investment in fit-outs, which makes leaving expensive
The location is central to how the business earns money

children.text: Back to Kharadi. Put rough probabilities on each tenant and the higher rent stops looking better. Assume over the next three years the startup has a 40% chance of leaving early and the multinational a 5% chance. Either exit costs about eight months of lost rent, eight months of CAM at ₹12,000 a month and two months' rent in brokerage.

body.label: Value of the stronger tenant over three years
body.context: Despite paying ₹10,000 a month less. The probabilities are illustrative, but the lesson holds: a lower rent from a reliable tenant often beats a higher rent from a risky one.

body.title: Stable tenant or higher rent?
body.prompt: A Noida flat owner has two applicants. Tenant X offers ₹30,000 a month and is likely to stay three years. Tenant Y offers ₹33,000 but, like the last two tenants at that rent, is likely to leave after a year. Assume Y's pattern repeats, so the flat changes tenants twice in three years, and each change costs three months' rent (two months empty plus one month's brokerage) at ₹33,000. How much more does X earn the owner over three years, in rupees?
body.explanation: Tenant X: 36 × ₹30,000 = ₹10,80,000. Tenant Y: 36 × ₹33,000 = ₹11,88,000, minus two changes × 3 × ₹33,000 = ₹1,98,000, leaving ₹9,90,000. X earns ₹90,000 more, before counting repainting and the hassle of two extra tenant searches.

body.title: How to check a commercial tenant's financials

children.text: Company filings:
the Ministry of Corporate Affairs portal shows a company's registration status, directors and filing history. Filed financial statements can be obtained from MCA records.
Listed tenants:
if the tenant or its parent is listed on NSE or BSE, screener.in gives you ten years of profits, debt and cash flow in minutes.
Credit ratings:
rated companies have public rating rationales on the CRISIL, ICRA and CARE websites explaining their strengths and risks.
GST status:
the GST portal's taxpayer search confirms whether a GSTIN is active and how long the business has been registered.
Unrated private tenants:
ask for audited financials, bank statements and, where possible, a larger security deposit, a parent or promoter guarantee, or a bank guarantee.

body.label: MCA: Company and LLP master data
body.description: Check a company tenant's registration status, directors and filing history on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs portal.

body.label: GST portal: Search taxpayer
body.description: Confirm a business tenant's GSTIN is active and see its registration date.

body.text: Police verification of tenants is required by police orders in many Indian cities, and owners who skip it can face penalties. It takes little time, often online, and gives you a verified identity record if something goes wrong. Always pair it with a written, properly stamped rent agreement.

body.title: The renewal negotiation
body.scenario: Sanjay Deshpande owns an office unit in Baner, Pune. The tenant, an established IT services firm, pays ₹1,30,000 a month after two escalations, and the lease ends next month. The tenant offers to renew for five years with a five-year lock-in, but only at ₹1,15,000 a month. Similar units nearby are renting at about ₹1,20,000. If the tenant leaves, Sanjay expects nine months of vacancy, CAM of ₹12,000 a month while empty, and brokerage of two months' rent.
body.prompt: Compare the next five years under both choices, and suggest how Sanjay should respond to the tenant's offer.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Why the cut? The unit is over-rented. ₹1,30,000 is above the ₹1,20,000 market rent, so the tenant has leverage.
2. Renew at ₹1,15,000 for 60 months: ₹1,15,000 × 60 = ₹69,00,000, fully locked in for five years.
3. Let the tenant go: nine months empty, then 51 months at ₹1,20,000 = ₹61,20,000. Minus CAM while empty (9 × ₹12,000 = ₹1,08,000) and brokerage (2 × ₹1,20,000 = ₹2,40,000) = ₹57,72,000. And the new tenant may not accept a five-year lock-in.
4. Renewing is worth about ₹11.3 lakh more over five years, even at below-market rent, with far less risk.
5. How to respond: accept the renewal in principle, but negotiate. Ask for ₹1,20,000 (the market rate) in return for the long lock-in, or accept ₹1,15,000 with a 15% escalation after three years. Keep the security deposit topped up to the new rent. A reliable, locked-in tenant is worth a small discount; it is not worth giving everything away.

body.title: Before you sign or buy into a lease
steps: Convert any step escalation into an equivalent annual rate and compare it with a straight annual increase.
Check whether the current rent is above, at or below today's market rent for similar units.
Note exactly when the lock-in ends and what notice the tenant must give after that.
For multi-tenant properties, calculate WALE and a weighted lock-in, not a simple average.
Verify the tenant: employment or company filings, credit rating, GST status and payment history.
Complete police verification and use a written, properly stamped and registered agreement where required.
Put rough probabilities on early exit and compare expected rent, not just headline rent.

cards.definition: A rent increase applied every year, such as 5% a year.
A larger increase at longer intervals, such as 15% every three years, equal to about 4.77% a year.
Contracted rent above current market rent, making a rent cut likely at renewal.
The advance warning needed to end a lease once the lock-in has passed.
An initial lease period when a tenant builds out interiors without paying rent.
Weighted average lease expiry: remaining lease years across tenants, weighted by rent.
Headline rent adjusted for the probability and cost of the tenant leaving early.

points: Escalation structure matters: 5% a year beats 15% every three years by about ₹7.3 lakh on a ₹1 lakh monthly rent over nine years.
Convert step escalations with (1 + step)^(1 ÷ years) − 1 to compare them fairly.
Escalations that outrun market rents create an over-rented property and a likely rent cut at renewal.
Only the lock-in period is truly guaranteed rent; after it, the tenant can leave with notice.
WALE weights remaining lease terms by rent and is the standard measure of income security for multi-tenant property and REITs.
Tenant quality should be judged on verifiable financial facts, never on personal characteristics.
A reliable tenant at a slightly lower rent often earns more in expected terms than a risky tenant paying more.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or legal advice. The people, properties, rents, probabilities and lease terms shown are illustrative. Tenancy laws, registration rules and police verification requirements vary by state and city, so read the actual lease and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a property lawyer before making any decision.
